findings.quote: Ions form when electrons move. The nucleus does not change, so $Z$ and $N$ stay the same.
findings.problem: This general statement fails for polyatomic ions, which the same section defines as ions ("An **ion** is an atom or a group of bonded atoms") and works in Example #8. The ammonium ion forms when ammonia accepts a hydrogen ion (NH3 + H+ gives NH4+), and the hydronium ion forms the same way: a proton moves, no electron is transferred, and the group gains a nucleus, so its proton count rises from 10 to 11. A student taught that every ion forms by electron movement with an unchanged nucleus will answer a question on how the ammonium ion forms wrongly. The base lesson limited the claim with "Ordinary ion formation changes electron count"; the rewrite dropped that limit. Trap #5 repeats the unlimited claim in "A positive ion has lost electrons, so it has fewer electrons than protons." (the count part is always true; the "has lost electrons" part fails for NH4+).
findings.source: IUPAC Gold Book, "ammonium" and "hydron" (cation formed by addition of a hydron to ammonia or water); base lesson 7032eec5 line 54; reader-rules "Added after the Sol audit" boundary and exception test; checklist B01
